q: What determines whether a project truly uses PRINCE2?
a: Application of all seven principles as guiding obligations.

q: What is the continued-justification test?
a: The project must remain desirable, viable and achievable; otherwise change or stop it.

q: Do sunk costs justify continuation?
a: No. Money already spent is not a reason for further investment.

q: May project parties have different justifications?
a: Yes. Customer, supplier and co-owners monitor their own financial or non-financial cases.

q: When does the team learn from experience?
a: Before, throughout and at the closure of the project.

q: What should happen to a lesson found during the project?
a: Record it and apply it as soon as practical when relevant.

q: Why is recording a lesson alone insufficient?
a: The principle requires improvements to be implemented and experience to be shared.

q: Why report lessons at closure?
a: So future projects and other teams can apply them.

q: Which interests does the project board represent?
a: Business, user and supplier interests.

q: What must the project organization clarify?
a: Roles, responsibilities, authority, mutual expectations and relationships.

q: May roles represent people outside the organization?
a: Yes. Suppliers and other stakeholders may be external.

q: Why are relationships part of the principle?
a: Structure alone does not create collaboration; relationships must be initiated, built and maintained.

q: What is a management stage?
a: The section managed at any one time by the project manager on behalf of the board.

q: How many stages must a PRINCE2 project have?
a: At least two: an initiation stage and at least one further stage.

q: How does stage length affect management?
a: A shorter stage increases control and management effort; a longer stage does the reverse.

q: How do sprints relate to stages?
a: One stage may contain several sprints; sprints support delivery, stages support control and decisions.

q: What is tolerance?
a: Permissible deviation from a plan target without escalation.

q: Which seven aspects use tolerance?
a: Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk.

q: When does a deviation become an exception?
a: When it is forecast to exceed the delegated tolerance.

q: At which levels is tolerance applied?
a: Project, stage and team or work-package levels.

q: What is a product in PRINCE2?
a: A tangible or intangible input or output that can be described, created and tested.

q: What are the four product types?
a: Management, specialist, the project product and external products.

q: What is an output-oriented project?
a: It defines products first and only then the activities needed to create them.

q: What do product descriptions support?
a: Estimates, resources, dependencies, scheduling, quality and acceptance.

q: Why tailor PRINCE2?
a: To make the method and controls proportionate to context, scale, complexity, importance, delivery, capability and risk.

q: Who recommends and who approves tailoring?
a: The project manager recommends; the project board is accountable and approves.

q: What does “information, not necessarily documents” mean?
a: Reliable management information is required, but its format may be tailored.

q: Which two extremes does tailoring avoid?
a: Unquestioning bureaucracy and “heroic” management based on improvisation.
